sourceSentences.text: These days, fear was layered well beneath calluses of experience.
Still, he gripped his shoulder bag tightly in one hand and held his brush out as he crept along.
There, on the wall, was a handprint with too-long fingers and what looked like claws.
Yes, it was taking a form.
Its prey must be close.
Farther along the narrow alley, by a bare wall, he found the nightmare: a thing of ink and shadow some seven feet tall.
It had fashioned two long arms that bent too many times, the elongated palms pressed against the wall, fingers spread.
Its head had sunk through the stone to peek into the room beyond.
The tall ones always unnerved him, particularly when they had long fingers.
He felt he’d seen figures like that in his own fragmented dreams—figments of terrors buried within.
His feet scraped the stones, and the thing heard and withdrew its head, wisps of formless blackness rising from it like ash from a smoldering fire.
No face though.
They never had faces—not unless something was going very wrong.
Instead they usually displayed a deeper blackness on the front of the head.
One that dripped dark liquid.
Like tears, or wax near a flame.
Painter immediately raised his mental protections, thinking calm thoughts.
This was the first and most important training.
The nightmares, like many predators that fed on minds, could sense thoughts and emotions.
They searched for the most powerful, raw ones to feed upon.
A placid mind was of little interest.
The thing turned and put its head through the wall again.
This building had no windows, which was foolish.
Nightmares could ignore walls.
In removing windows, the occupants trapped themselves more fully in the boxes of their homes, feeding their claustrophobia—and making the jobs of the painters more difficult.
Painter moved carefully, slowly, taking a canvas—a good three-foot by three-foot piece of thick cloth on a frame—from his shoulder bag.
He set it on the ground in front of him.
His jar of ink followed—black and runny.
Nightmare painters always worked in black on white, no colors, as you wanted something that mimicked the look of a nightmare.
The ink blend was designed to give excellent gradations in the grey and black.
Not that Painter bothered with that much nuance these days.
He dipped the brush in the ink and knelt above his canvas, then paused, gazing at the nightmare.
The blackness continued to steam off it, and its shape was still fairly indistinct.
This was probably only its first or second trip into the city.
It took a good dozen trips before a nightmare had enough substance to be dangerous—and they had to return to the shroud each time to renew, lest they evaporate away.
Judging by its appearance, this one was fairly new.
It probably couldn’t hurt him.
Probably.
And here was the crux of why painters were so important, yet so disposable.
Their job was essential, but not urgent.
As long as a nightmare was discovered within its first ten or so trips into the city, it could be neutralized.
That almost always happened.
Painter was good at controlling his fear with thoughts like these.
That was part of his training—very pragmatic.
Once his breathing calmed, he tried to consider what the nightmare looked like, what its shape could have been.
Supposedly if you picked something that the entity already resembled, then painted that, you would have more power over it.
He had trouble with this.
Or rather, during the last few months it had felt like more trouble than it was worth.
So today he settled on the shape of a small bamboo thicket and began painting.
The thing had spindly arms, after all.
Those were kind of like bamboo.
He’d practiced a great number of bamboo stalks.
In fact, you could say that Painter had a certain scientific precision in the way he drew each segment—a little sideways flourish at the start, followed by a long line.
You let the brush linger a moment so that when you raised it, the blot the brush left formed the end knob of the bamboo segment.
You could create each in a single stroke.
It was efficient, and these days that seemed most important to him.
As he painted, he fixed the shape in his mind—a central powerful image.
As usual such deliberate thought drew the thing’s attention.
It hesitated, then pulled its head out from the wall and turned in his direction, its face dripping its own ink.
It moved toward him, walking on its arms, but those had grown more round.
With knobbed segments.
Painter continued.
Stroke.
Flourish.
Leaves made with quick flips of the brush, blacker than the main body of the bamboo.
Similar protrusions appeared on the arms of the thing as it drew closer.
It also shrank in upon itself as he painted a pot at the bottom.
The painting captured the thing.
Diverted it.
So that by the time it reached him, the transformation was fully in effect.
He never lost himself in the painting these days.
After all, he told himself, he had a job to do.
And he did that job well.
As he finished, the thing even adopted some of the sounds of bamboo—the soft rattle of stalks beating against one another to accompany the omnipresent buzz of the hion lines above.
He lifted his brush, leaving a perfect bamboo painting on his canvas, mimicked by the thing in the alley, leaves brushing the walls.
Then, with a sound very much like a sigh, the nightmare dispersed.
He’d deliberately transformed it into a harmless shape—and now, trapped as it was, it couldn’t flee to the shroud to regain strength.
Instead, like water trapped on a hot plate, it just…evaporated.
Soon Painter was alone in the alley.
He packed up his things, sliding the canvas back into the large bag, alongside three unused ones.
Then he returned to his patrol.

Следом достал банку жидкой чёрной туши.

Наверное.

Отвлекла его.

В конце концов, напоминал он себе, ему поручено дело.

испарился.
Вскоре Художник снова остался в переулке один.
Он собрал вещи, засунув холст в большую сумку рядом с тремя неиспользованными, и вернулся к обходу.

Картина захватила существо. Отвлекла его. И к тому времени, когда оно приблизилось, превращение полностью завершилось.

Теперь Художник никогда не забывался в работе. В конце концов, напоминал он себе, ему поручено дело. И он хорошо его выполняет. Когда картина была почти готова, существо переняло даже звуки бамбука — тихое постукивание стеблей друг о друга, сопровождавшее постоянное гудение линий хиона над головой.

Он поднял кисть. На холсте остался безупречный бамбук, а существо в переулке повторяло картину, задевая листьями стены. Затем со звуком, очень похожим на вздох, кошмар рассеялся. Художник намеренно придал ему безобидную форму — и теперь, запертый в ней, он не мог бежать к Завесе за силой. Как вода, оставленная на раскалённой плите, он просто… испарился.
Вскоре Художник снова остался в переулке один. Он собрал вещи, засунув холст в большую сумку рядом с тремя неиспользованными, и вернулся к обходу.

paragraphPairs.sourceText: These days, fear was layered well beneath calluses of experience. Still, he gripped his shoulder bag tightly in one hand and held his brush out as he crept along. There, on the wall, was a handprint with too-long fingers and what looked like claws. Yes, it was taking a form. Its prey must be close.
paragraphPairs.translatedText: Теперь страх лежал глубоко под мозолями опыта. И всё же Художник крепко сжимал одной рукой сумку на плече, а другую вытянул вперёд с кистью, осторожно продвигаясь дальше. Там, на стене, отпечаталась ладонь со слишком длинными пальцами и чем-то похожим на когти. Да, существо обретало форму. Его жертва должна быть рядом.

paragraphPairs.sourceText: Farther along the narrow alley, by a bare wall, he found the nightmare: a thing of ink and shadow some seven feet tall. It had fashioned two long arms that bent too many times, the elongated palms pressed against the wall, fingers spread. Its head had sunk through the stone to peek into the room beyond.

paragraphPairs.sourceText: The tall ones always unnerved him, particularly when they had long fingers. He felt he’d seen figures like that in his own fragmented dreams—figments of terrors buried within. His feet scraped the stones, and the thing heard and withdrew its head, wisps of formless blackness rising from it like ash from a smoldering fire.
paragraphPairs.translatedText: Высокие кошмары всегда тревожили его, особенно длиннопалые. Ему казалось, что подобные фигуры встречались в его собственных обрывочных снах — порождения похороненных внутри страхов. Подошва заскребла по камню; существо услышало звук и вытащило голову, а от него поднялись клочья бесформенной черноты, как пепел от тлеющего костра.

paragraphPairs.sourceText: Painter immediately raised his mental protections, thinking calm thoughts. This was the first and most important training. The nightmares, like many predators that fed on minds, could sense thoughts and emotions. They searched for the most powerful, raw ones to feed upon. A placid mind was of little interest.

Кошмары, подобно многим хищникам, питающимся разумом, чувствовали мысли и эмоции. Они искали самые сильные, самые обнажённые чувства, чтобы поживиться ими. Безмятежный разум их почти не интересовал.

paragraphPairs.sourceText: Painter moved carefully, slowly, taking a canvas—a good three-foot by three-foot piece of thick cloth on a frame—from his shoulder bag. He set it on the ground in front of him. His jar of ink followed—black and runny. Nightmare painters always worked in black on white, no colors, as you wanted something that mimicked the look of a nightmare. The ink blend was designed to give excellent gradations in the grey and black. Not that Painter bothered with that much nuance these days.

Следом достал банку жидкой чёрной туши. Художники кошмаров всегда работали чёрным по белому, без красок: изображение должно было походить на сам кошмар. paragraphPairs.sourceText: He dipped the brush in the ink and knelt above his canvas, then paused, gazing at the nightmare. The blackness continued to steam off it, and its shape was still fairly indistinct. This was probably only its first or second trip into the city. It took a good dozen trips before a nightmare had enough substance to be dangerous—and they had to return to the shroud each time to renew, lest they evaporate away.
paragraphPairs.translatedText: Он обмакнул кисть в тушь, опустился на колени над холстом и замер, разглядывая кошмар. Чернота продолжала испаряться с его тела, а очертания оставались довольно неопределёнными. Вероятно, существо лишь в первый или второй раз пробралось в город. Кошмару требовалось добрых двенадцать вылазок, чтобы обрести достаточно вещества и стать опасным; после каждой он должен был возвращаться в Завесу и обновляться, иначе попросту испарился бы.

paragraphPairs.sourceText: Painter was good at controlling his fear with thoughts like these. That was part of his training—very pragmatic. Once his breathing calmed, he tried to consider what the nightmare looked like, what its shape could have been. Supposedly if you picked something that the entity already resembled, then painted that, you would have more power over it. He had trouble with this. Or rather, during the last few months it had felt like more trouble than it was worth.
paragraphPairs.translatedText: Такие мысли помогали Художнику усмирять страх. Это тоже входило в обучение — весьма практичный приём. Когда дыхание выровнялось, он попытался понять, на что похож кошмар, какую форму мог бы принять. Считалось, что если выбрать нечто, что уже напоминает сущность, и нарисовать это, власть над ней усилится. Художнику это давалось трудно. Вернее, последние несколько месяцев усилия казались неоправданными.

paragraphPairs.sourceText: It was efficient, and these days that seemed most important to him. As he painted, he fixed the shape in his mind—a central powerful image. As he finished, the thing even adopted some of the sounds of bamboo—the soft rattle of stalks beating against one another to accompany the omnipresent buzz of the hion lines above.

paragraphPairs.sourceText: He lifted his brush, leaving a perfect bamboo painting on his canvas, mimicked by the thing in the alley, leaves brushing the walls. Then, with a sound very much like a sigh, the nightmare dispersed. He’d deliberately transformed it into a harmless shape—and now, trapped as it was, it couldn’t flee to the shroud to regain strength. Instead, like water trapped on a hot plate, it just…evaporated.
paragraphPairs.translatedText: Он поднял кисть. На холсте остался безупречный бамбук, а существо в переулке повторяло картину, задевая листьями стены. Затем со звуком, очень похожим на вздох, кошмар рассеялся. Художник намеренно придал ему безобидную форму — и теперь, запертый в ней, он не мог бежать к Завесе за силой. Как вода, оставленная на раскалённой плите, он просто… испарился.
